title: 8. Stage 2 Technical Structure, Institutional Flow & Momentum Setup

epigraph.quote: Underwriting Rule: a chart cannot tell you what a business is worth. It can only tell you who is in a hurry, and whether that person is buying or selling.
epigraph.author: Research Desk house maxim

web_blocks.html: The first seven chapters judged the business. This one judges the tape, and the tape disagrees with the business on timing. On the verified 12 Nov 2026 NSE ledger, MPS closed at ₹2,297.00 (+1.48% on the day, -8.70% over a month). The ledger classifies it as Stage 3 (Topping / Pullback) [90]. The TradingView pull taken after the 13 Nov close shows ₹2,259.30 (-1.64%). Its classifier says Stage 4, entry posture AVOID_STAGE4_OR_BROKEN, timing gate CAP_REJECTED [91]. We date this report by the verified ledger, so ₹2,297.00 is the reference price. The 13 Nov figure is a later print that the ledger has not yet verified. We never merge the two. Our reading is that MPS sits exactly on the Stage 3 / Stage 4 boundary. The stricter of the two readings governs the timing gate.

A word on the method before the numbers. Stan Weinstein's stage analysis sorts every stock into four phases: base, advance, top and decline. It uses the 30-week moving average as the referee. Price above a rising 30-week line is strength. Price whipsawing around a flattening line is basing or topping. Price below a falling line is trouble [92]. The rule most useful to a quality-business investor is what Weinstein calls the oath. Do not buy into a Stage 4 decline, however good the story sounds. Wait for a Stage 1 base before even considering it [92]. Stage 3 differs from a Stage 1 base in what came before it, which is an advance and not a decline. It also brings heavy two-sided volume. Nothing on this page says MPS is a bad business. It says the stock is not yet in the phase where Weinstein would put new money to work. The price history in this chapter shows why that discipline matters for this stock.

web_blocks.caption: What each moving average says about MPS now (ledger close ₹2,297.00 on 12 Nov; 13 Nov print ₹2,259.30)
web_blocks.takeaway: On the 13 Nov print, four of the five averages sit above the price. Only the 200-day sits below. The 30-week line is being tested rather than defended. The 200-day is the next structural floor, and the entry zone is built on it. Ledger values are as of 12 Nov. The weekly values and the 13 Nov distances come from the TradingView pull [90, 91]. The compiled technical table strikes its extension figures on the 13 Nov print (₹2,259.30). They are -6.49% from the 10-week EMA and -9.68% from the 50-day. On the 12 Nov close (₹2,297.00) the same gaps are -4.9% and -8.2%, against the snapshot's 10-week EMA (₹2,416.11) and 50-day (₹2,501.56).

The shelf. Price is sitting on it, not above it. A rising average with price beneath it is the textbook Stage 3 to Stage 4 transition zone.
6.49% below on the 13 Nov print (4.9% below on the 12 Nov close)

Confirms that the weekly structure is a coiled shelf, with both weekly averages bunched at roughly ₹2,262 to ₹2,268.

web_blocks.html: Put the four lines together. The stock has not yet broken its long-term trend, but it has lost its short-term one. That is why the ledger says Stage 3 and the snapshot says Stage 4. Both are defensible. The ledger works on daily averages. Price below a falling 50-day and above a rising 200-day is, by construction, the pullback-or-top zone [90]. The snapshot classifier works on the weekly shelf. A close below the 30-week SMA plus a weak trend means Stage 4 [91]. Our own recomputation from the daily history adds a detail. The weekly close of 6 Nov (₹2,232.90) was already marginally under the 30-week average (about ₹2,245). So two of the last three weekly closes sit below the line, each by a hair. The 30-week average itself has not yet turned down. That is the honest argument for calling this a boundary rather than a confirmed decline. We still take the stricter reading for the timing gate, because the cost of being wrong is asymmetric. If we wait on a quality stock and it rebounds from the zone, we lose a few per cent of upside. If we enter and the stock confirms Stage 4, we can lose the 20% to 30% that the shelf structure below it implies.

web_blocks.caption: Multi-timeframe read: 1W / 1D / 4H (TradingView pull, 13 Nov 2026, close ₹2,259.30)
web_blocks.takeaway: Momentum is soft on every frame but not washed out. RSI of 40.7 to 46.55 is neither oversold nor a base. The tool's auto-text calls the setup 'DISLOCATION_AT_MAJOR_SHELF'. It says price is 'stabilising above' the ₹2,262.01 shelf with 4H momentum 'turning up'. The print contradicts both phrases. It is 0.12% below the shelf, below the 4H 20-period EMA the text says it is above, and the tool's own 4H turn flag is false. Read it as price on the shelf. A weekly close further below the shelf would confirm Stage 4 [91].
rows: The 'major shelf' is the 30-week SMA at ₹2,262.01; perf: 3M -17.85%, 6M +38.33%, 1Y -0.65%
The decisive frame. Price on the shelf, momentum mid-range, short average rolling over.
ATR14 ₹110.16 (about 4.9% of price); Bollinger-band width 12.04% (the tool does not state its frame)
Below every short average, above the 200-day. Lower highs since 7 Aug. Next structural support is the 200-day and S1, 8% to 9% down.
Short-term bounce attempts are failing under the 4H EMA20. No turn has been confirmed.

web_blocks.html: The tool also generates an options idea, a call-spread window toward the 50-day average. We set that aside. MPS has no NSE futures-and-options contract, and the tool itself marks the stock NOT_OPTIONABLE_OR_ILLIQUID. Any view on this name can only be expressed in the cash equity. No derivative overlay exists to hedge or leverage the timing risk [91].

web_blocks.takeaway: Sellers have been heavier than buyers on average, but at tiny absolute size. Volume has collapsed to roughly a third of its rally-period level. This is distribution into a thin market, not capitulation. The only candle that looks like capitulation is the 4 Nov results day. The stock bounced from its low rather than closing on it [90].

web_blocks.html: Two features of that table deserve emphasis. First, the volume ratio is a mild warning. A 1.33x skew of down-day volume over up-day volume is what Weinstein would call churn: stock changing hands on both sides without progress [92]. It is nowhere near the 2x to 3x surge on rising prices that he demands before calling a breakout. Second, the 4 Nov session is the closest thing this stock has had to a flush. The company raised its FY27 EBITDA floor that day. Yet the shares traded 8.3% below the previous close intraday and then recovered. A guidance raise that the stock cannot hold is a classic late-distribution sign. We treat the quick recovery as evidence that the ₹2,150 area has buyers. It is not proof that the low is in.

web_blocks.takeaway: The Mar to Aug advance ran +114.5% on daily closes, from ₹1,366.70 on 9 Mar to ₹2,931.20 on 7 Aug. At the 12 Nov close the stock has given back 40.5% of that leg. At the 13 Nov print it has given back 42.9%. The 50% retracement lands at ₹2,148.95, almost exactly on the top of our entry zone. The 61.8% level at ₹1,964.34 sits below the stop. That is why a daily close below ₹2,005 would signal more than a normal pullback [90].

web_blocks.html: Now the liquidity point, because it matters more here than the chart. MPS has about 17.1 million shares in issue. The promoter group (ADI BPO Services) holds 68.34%, so the free float is roughly 31.7%. That is worth about ₹1,244 Cr at the ledger close [93]. The stock trades about 15,000 to 19,000 shares a day, or roughly ₹3.5 Cr to ₹4.5 Cr on recent averages. For a portfolio of this size that is not a binding constraint. The half-tier first fill of about 3.25% of NAV is roughly ₹1.39 lakh, or about 65 whole shares. That is well under 1% of one average day's value. Liquidity does matter for execution. The daily ATR is ₹116 (5.1% of price), the book is thin, and some sessions total only 6,719 shares. A single order can gap through a level and print a spike. We therefore recommend limit prices rather than market orders on any entry or exit. Work each tranche over several sessions rather than in one clip. The ₹2,005 stop is a daily close, not an intraday print. On 27 Oct the stock traded down to ₹2,152.20 and closed at ₹2,218.60. A stop that fires on an intraday spike in a thin tape is a donation to the market maker.

web_blocks.caption: Who owns the free float: selected quarters from the shareholding pattern (promoter holding constant at 68.34%)
web_blocks.takeaway: Foreign institutions have sold about 60% of their stake since December 2023 (3.71% to 1.49%). Domestic institutions have more than tripled theirs from a tiny base (0.56% to 2.11%). The number of shareholders is up 67% to 26,333. The rise to ₹2,931 was therefore carried largely by retail and a few domestic funds, not by foreign money. That is a thin, price-sensitive buyer base [93].

web_blocks.html: What does that say about the marginal buyer? Combined FII and DII ownership went from 4.27% to 3.60% over the period. Institutions in aggregate are therefore net sellers of the free float since the end of 2023. Domestic funds did begin accumulating from the December 2025 quarter, a few months before the shares made their low [93]. The Sep 2026 quarter ended with the stock near ₹2,700. The next filing (Dec 2026) will show who bought and sold the 15% fall since. Two readings are possible. The bullish one is that low foreign ownership means little overhang and room for a re-rating once growth is recognised. The cautious one is that institutions own only 3.6% and 31.7% of the equity is in public hands. Each rally then depends on retail enthusiasm, and each decline meets thin bids. We do not need to choose. We only note that no heavy institutional sponsor is visible in the Weinstein sense. There is no obvious large buyer to defend a break of the shelf. ADI BPO's amalgamation into MPS is, on management's account, a cancellation and re-issue of the same number of shares. It leaves public holders undiluted. But the NCLT outcome from the 4 Nov hearing is unconfirmed. Until it lands, the free-float question is not fully closed.

web_blocks.caption: Relative strength: MPS against the Nifty and against its listed peers (all peers in Stage 4)
web_blocks.takeaway: Over a year MPS is flat (-0.65%), while Datamatics, NIIT Learning Systems and Newgen are down 18% to 56%. Over six months it is the only name in the set that is up (+38.33%). Over three months the gap has closed: -17.85% against -16.56%, -29.20% and -18.22%. Relative strength against the Nifty is -26.74% over 28 days and -22.76% over 63 days. MPS is the leader of a collapsing group that has itself started to roll over. TheWrap's weekly Stage 2 universe (465 stocks, as of 8 Nov 2026) contains none of the four [91, 94].

web_blocks.html: The market backdrop is no help and no hindrance. The ledger's regime reading is Uptrend (narrow breadth). 61.0% of the screened universe sits above its 50-day average, and the Nifty shows 4 distribution days [90]. TheWrap's list shows 465 Indian stocks in Stage 2 as of 8 Nov (328 continuing, 91 re-entries, 46 new). Only 28% of its IT Services group qualifies, and MPS is not among the 465 [94]. Many stocks have better technical credentials. That is the practical reason the opportunity cost of waiting is low.

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: A relative-strength leader that has stopped leading
paragraphs: It is tempting to read the peer table as a compliment. MPS held its value while three competitors lost a fifth to a half of theirs. Surely the market is voting for the better business. I think that is half right. The market did separate MPS from its peers for most of the year. The ROCE, margin and debt numbers in chapters 4 and 6 explain why.

But relative strength measures what has happened. Over the last three months MPS has fallen as hard as the group it outran. A leader that stops leading is not a laggard. It is no longer the stock to chase. That is the point of Stage 3. The best names are the last to crack, and they crack from a higher price.

web_blocks.caption: Price cycles since 2015 (weekly closes) matched to the business events from Pass 1 and the trailing-FY-EPS P/E at each turn
web_blocks.takeaway: Three drawdowns of 50% or more (-57.7%, -67.5%, -51.9%) in eleven years, and two of the three began at a trailing P/E of 31x or higher. The business events line up with the turns. Each time, though, the price move was several times larger than the earnings change, because the multiple did most of the work. Today's 22.7x equals the five-year median. The full weekly band since Jun 2016 has a median of 17.6x, a 75th percentile of 23.0x and a maximum of 41.7x [90, 1].
rows: FY15 QIP cash sat idle, and ROCE fell from 49% to 23%. FY18 sales fell 8%. Then the Tata Interactive acquisition (31 May 2018) took the operating margin from 33% to 26% in FY19.
FY19 sales rose 36% from the consolidated acquisition. The business had become cheap relative to its cash generation, and the stock staged a relief rally.

FY20 was the trough. Price cuts, vendor consolidation and a platform customer moving work to its captive took FY20 revenue to ₹334 Cr and cut EBITDA by ₹11 Cr. Then came the Covid shock in March 2020.

HighWire (Jul 2020) lifted platforms from 16% to 33% of revenue. Then came the eLearning restructuring, the FY22 buyback, EI Design, Liberate and AJE (Feb 2024). FY25 sales rose 33% and ROCE reached about 41%. Even in this run the stock fell about 33% in May 2022.

AJE revenue was cut by more than a quarter. FY26 sales rose 5.6% and Corporate Learning fell 16.5%. There was no final dividend. The Unbound deal came on 9 Feb 2026. Peers that have since fallen 18% to 56% over a year point to a sector-wide de-rating.
Q1 FY27 revenue was ₹224.24 Cr (+20.4%), EBITDA ₹76.96 Cr at 34.3%, and Research margin 45.1%. The stock re-rated from 16x to 29x on one quarter. The close high came on a 6.1% gain on 130,151 shares.
Q2 FY27 beat and the FY27 EBITDA floor was raised to at least ₹310 Cr. The multiple compressed anyway. Price is down 20.7% from the Mar 2025 peak.

web_blocks.html: The cycle table is the most important evidence in this chapter for how much to put on and how patient to be. The stock has gone through three drawdowns of 50% or more since 2015. Each came while the business was either executing a strategy change (Tata Interactive, the FY20 reset) or being re-rated by the market (2025 to 2026). The stock has also produced one of the strongest runs on the exchange, +1,416% in 59 months. Both are true of the same stock. This is a high-beta compounder in the literal sense. The compounding comes with drawdowns that a 6.5% tier cap cannot absorb without pain. That is why our rule for MPS is a first fill capped at half the tier cap, about 3.25% of NAV if both tranches fill. It is split into two unequal tranches. Two-thirds is the core order at ₹2,070. The smaller third at ₹2,150 is conditional. The balance waits for a confirmed base and a fresh re-underwrite. At the 12 Nov close the stock is already 21.6% off its high, so some of the reset has happened. But the Mar 2025 to Mar 2026 leg shows what the full version looks like. The trailing P/E went from 41.7x to 16.0x in 11 months.

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: What three 50% drawdowns do to a position
paragraphs: If you had bought at the ₹1,022 peak in 2015, you would not have seen a weekly close above it again until February 2023. If you had bought at ₹588 in November 2019, you would have lost two-thirds of it in under five months. Yet someone who held through all of it from March 2020 would show a 26.1% annual return over five years (price only, to 12 Nov 2026). Both statements are true. They are the whole argument for patience with this stock.

I do not read the cycle table as a reason to avoid MPS. I read it as a reason to choose my own entry price instead of letting the market choose it for me. It is also a reason to size so that a 50% fall is an inconvenience rather than a crisis.

web_blocks.html: Here is the entry-zone logic, level by level. The zone is ₹2,070.00 to ₹2,150.00. Its upper edge is the 20-day swing low of ₹2,152.20. That level was tested on 27 Oct and again, within ₹3, on 4 Nov. It also coincides with the 50% retracement at ₹2,148.95. Its lower edge is the rising 200-day average at ₹2,069.06 and TradingView's monthly S1 at ₹2,065.93. The snapshot's own support band of ₹2,034.94 to ₹2,096.92 brackets the same area [91]. Four independent anchors cluster in a 4% band, which is what a real support area looks like. The stop is a daily close below ₹2,005.00. It sits below the 200-day by about half an ATR and below the snapshot's ₹2,010.85. It also lies above the 61.8% retracement at ₹1,964.34. The distance from ₹2,150 to ₹2,005 is 6.74% (1.25 ATR). That is tight enough to cap the loss and wide enough that normal noise should not trigger it. Do not confuse the stop with the Stage 4 signal. A weekly close below the 30-week average (₹2,262.01) is the Stage 4 confirmation. A daily close below ₹2,005.00 is the exit.

Now the reward-to-risk. We test the base value on two earnings bases. Our ten-year P/E band is built on the last reported fiscal-year EPS. At a Nov 2027 value date, that basis means FY27E EPS. The band's multiples (14x, 18x, 22x) then give a base value of ₹2,241. Call that basis A, the stress case. Valuing on last-twelve-months EPS at the value date gives a base value of ₹2,410, which is 18x EPS of ₹133.9. Call that basis B, our central case. Markets price on current earnings and the band uses a lagging EPS, so basis A understates what the market usually pays. Against the ₹2,005 stop, reward-to-risk at ₹2,070 is 2.63:1 on basis A and 5.23:1 on basis B. At ₹2,150 it is 0.63:1 on basis A and 1.79:1 on basis B. At the ledger close of ₹2,297.00 it is -0.19:1 and 0.39:1. At the 13 Nov print of ₹2,259.30 it is -0.07:1 and 0.59:1. The 1.5:1 hurdle is met on both bases only at ₹2,070. The ₹2,150 tranche clears it on basis B alone. It needs a base value of at least ₹2,367.50. Basis B clears that line by 1.8%, and basis A misses it by ₹126.50. The probability-weighted value is ₹2,254 on basis A and ₹2,440 on basis B. From ₹2,297.00 that is -1.9% and +6.2%. From ₹2,150 it is +4.8% and +13.5%. From ₹2,070 it is +8.9% and +17.9%. That is the whole reason for waiting. The business passes, and the price does not yet. The 25/50/25 weights are a judgment. Moving to 35/45/20 would lower the basis B weighted value to about ₹2,317. The decision does not depend on the weights, because the rule is the reward-to-risk at the support zone.

How can we hold the Stage 4 reading and still post limit prices? They are two different trades. The Stage 4 reading forbids buying at the current price or on a bounce. Weinstein's oath applies there [92]. The ₹2,070 order is the core of the plan. It sits at the rising 200-day average (₹2,069.06), which stood at ₹1,918.86 63 sessions ago. The long-term uptrend is intact at that level. The order clears 1.5:1 on both earnings bases (2.63:1 and 5.23:1). The ₹2,150 order is smaller and conditional. It is placed only if the re-derived base value is at least ₹2,367.50 on the day. Both are half-size, counter-trend support entries. We abandon them if the daily close breaks ₹2,005. Neither is a Stage 2 entry. Neither claims that the trend has turned.

The sizing follows from the two bases. The starter is about 3.25% of NAV (₹1,39,479 on net worth of ₹42,91,664), split into two unequal parts. Two-thirds, about ₹92,986 or 2.17% of NAV, is the core order at ₹2,070. It buys 44 whole shares for ₹91,080. One-third, about ₹46,493 or 1.08% of NAV, is the conditional order at ₹2,150. It buys 21 shares for ₹45,150. Place it only if, on the day, the base value re-run with the latest quarter's results and guidance is at least ₹2,367.50 on basis A. That needs FY27E EPS of about ₹131.5, which means FY27 EBITDA of roughly ₹331 Cr or more. Otherwise skip it and keep the cash. If it is skipped, the first fill is about 2.17% of NAV, not 3.25%. If both fill, the total is 65 shares for ₹1,36,230 (3.17% of NAV) at a blended ₹2,095.85. A daily close below ₹2,005 would then lose about ₹5,905, roughly 14 bps of NAV. At the bear value of ₹1,630 the loss would be about ₹30,280, or 0.71% of NAV. For scale, a full 6.5% position filled at ₹2,150 is 129 shares, and its loss at ₹1,630 would be ₹67,080. That is why the rest of the tier cap is not released without a fresh re-underwrite.

web_blocks.caption: Decision ladder: what the tape must do, and what we would do about it
web_blocks.takeaway: There are two ways back into the stock. One is a pullback into the support zone with the stop in place. The other is a confirmed new base that proves the decline is over, followed by a fresh re-underwrite. A daily close below ₹2,005 is the third state. In that case the same discipline says step aside, not average down [92, 91].
rows: Price trades into ₹2,070 to ₹2,150, preferably on lighter volume with a daily close back above the 4H and 10-day averages

Two-thirds (about 2.17% of NAV, 44 shares) at ₹2,070 is the core order. One-third (about 1.08%, 21 shares) at ₹2,150 is placed only if the re-derived base value is at least ₹2,367.50 on the year-end basis (about ₹331 Cr FY27 EBITDA). Stop: daily close below ₹2,005.
B. Stage 2 re-entry without a dip
Weekly close above the 30-week average with the 10-week EMA turning up and volume expanding. Or a weekly close above the falling 50-day average (about ₹2,500) with the 30-week average rising.

Not an automatic add, and it does not release the rest of the 6.5% cap. It re-opens the file for a re-underwrite. The base value is re-derived from the latest results, the stop is re-based, and any add must clear 1.5:1 from the add price to the new stop. The current bases (₹2,410 and ₹2,241) are both below ₹2,500, so at that price today's numbers give a negative reward.
Daily close below ₹2,005 (the stop). A weekly close below the 30-week average (₹2,262.01) is the separate Stage 4 confirmation signal.
Stage 4 confirmed: next shelves ₹1,810.97 (TradingView S2), then ₹1,336 to ₹1,393 (the Mar 2026 base). Cancel the alert and do not average down.
Neither level is reached for weeks while volume stays near 0.25x
No position. The base-building that Weinstein requires takes time; the opportunity cost is low.

web_blocks.html: Scenario C deserves a plain description. If the daily close breaks ₹2,005, the loss is about 6.7% from ₹2,150 and 3.1% from ₹2,070. The technical picture also changes character. The 200-day, the last intact long-term average, would be lost, and the weekly 30-week line would be falling. The nearest shelf is TradingView's S2 at ₹1,810.97, which is 9.7% below the stop. Below that, the March 2026 base at ₹1,336 to ₹1,393 is where the stock turned the last time the market doubted the business. We do not forecast that. We simply refuse to hold a plan that depends on it not happening. Management's own words on capital allocation show why this matters to the stock and not just to the chart. The CEO told the Q2 FY27 call, “capital must earn its return within 12 months, or it goes back to the shareholders” [2]. The same call said distributions resume only after acquisition capital is deployed. Until then, shareholders have no yield to be paid for waiting.

What would change our technical view. Upgrade (Stage 2 re-entry or confirmed support): a weekly close above the 30-week average (₹2,262.01) with the 10-week EMA (₹2,416.11) turning up. Weekly volume should be at least 2x the recent 20,000-share-a-day norm in the breakout week. A weekly close above the falling 50-day average (about ₹2,500), with the 30-week average rising, would also qualify. Either event re-opens the file for a fresh re-underwrite. It does not release the rest of the 6.5% cap. The base value is re-derived from the latest results, the stop is re-based to the new base and 200-day, and any add must clear 1.5:1 from the add price to the new stop. At ₹2,500 the current base values (₹2,410 and ₹2,241) give a negative reward. Entry trigger: price inside ₹2,070 to ₹2,150, with volume drying up (below about 0.5x the 20-day average) and no daily close under ₹2,005. The ₹2,070 order is the core. The ₹2,150 order is conditional on a re-derived base value of at least ₹2,367.50 on the year-end basis. Downgrade (Stage 4 confirmed): a weekly close clearly below the 30-week average, or a daily close below ₹2,005. A second heavy-volume down session (above 40,000 shares) that closes under ₹2,150 without a reversal would also count. Alert flow: the Dec 2026 shareholding filing should show whether domestic institutions kept buying below ₹2,700. A rise above 2.5% would be the first sign of a real sponsor.

Everything in this chapter feeds one conclusion, which chapter 9 turns into the verdict. The business is a pass. The tape is a Stage 3 / Stage 4 boundary with distribution volume and a falling 50-day average. The sensible plan is to wait for the support zone or a confirmed base. Chapter 9 puts the numbers behind the sizing and the three-horizon call. It also explains why the reviewed capital stays in cash until one of the triggers above is met.

book_paragraphs: Let me start this chapter by admitting something. Everything we have done up to now was about the business, and you and I came away from it with a company that earns a 38.7 per cent return on capital, carries no bank debt and has just raised its own guidance. A reasonable person would ask why we are not simply buying it. This chapter is the answer, and it is not about the company at all. It is about the stock, which is a different animal.

Picture the stock on a weekly chart. For five months it ran from ₹1,367 to ₹2,931, a gain of 114 per cent. Then on 7 August it made its high, on heavy volume, on a good day. In the fourteen weeks since, it has drifted down to ₹2,297, a fall of about 22 per cent. That is not a crash. It is something subtler and, in my experience, more dangerous: a slow leak in which nothing dramatic happens and yet the bid keeps stepping back a few rupees at a time.

How do I know it is a leak and not a rest? Three things. The fifty-day average, which was ₹2,704 three weeks ago, is now ₹2,517 and falling. The ledger counts nine distribution days in the last twenty-five sessions, which are days when the price falls on higher volume than usual. And when I split the sessions since the peak into up days and down days, the down days average about 22,000 shares and the up days about 17,000. The sellers are, on balance, a third more energetic than the buyers.

Now I want you to hold the other side of the picture in your head too, because honest technical work always has one. The stock is still above its rising 200-day average. The long-term trend has not been broken. The average volume has fallen by about two-thirds from the rally days, which means the selling is not panicked. On 4 November, the day of the results, the shares dipped to ₹2,155, more than 8 per cent below the prior close, and the buyers appeared. The very same level had held on 27 October. A level that is tested twice and holds twice is worth writing down.

So where does that leave us on the Weinstein map? The ledger, which looks at daily averages, says Stage 3: topping, pulling back. The 13 November snapshot, which looks at the weekly 30-week average, says Stage 4, because the shares closed at ₹2,259.30, a mere 0.12 per cent below that average of ₹2,262.01. I will be frank with you: this is a boundary, not a verdict. The thirty-week average is still rising, so the long-term uptrend is technically intact. But when two reasonable measures disagree and one of them says decline, I let the stricter one decide the timing. A mistaken wait costs a little upside. A mistaken entry costs a lot more.

Let me give you the four lines I look at, in plain words, because they are the vocabulary of this whole chapter. The thirty-week average is the referee: Stan Weinstein built his method around it, and it is simply the average of the last thirty weekly closes, about seven months of trading. It stands at ₹2,262 and the price is sitting on it. The ten-week average is the quick line, and it is at ₹2,416 and has been falling for six weeks. The fifty-day average, at roughly ₹2,500, is the ceiling the stock would have to reclaim to say the fall is over. And the two-hundred-day average, at about ₹2,070, is the floor under everything. Three of those lines are above the price and one is below. A stock in that arrangement is not in trouble yet, but it is not in a place where I would put new money.

One more correction, because it will save you from a trap. The options tool that supplied the weekly numbers wrote that the stock is stabilising above the shelf, with short-term momentum turning up. Look at its own data: the price is on the shelf, slightly under it, below the four-hour average it says it is above, and its own turn flag is set to false. Automatic commentary is a convenience, not a source. The numbers, not the sentences, are what I trust. And while we are on the tools, MPS has no futures and options contract on the NSE, so there is no clever derivative to express this view with. Cash equity is the only instrument.

There is also the question of where we are in the larger swing. Take the advance from the March low of ₹1,367 to the August high of ₹2,931. The market has so far given back about 40 per cent of it, and halfway down that climb, at ₹2,149, is almost exactly the top of the zone I will tell you about shortly. If the stock gave back sixty-two per cent, to ₹1,964, it would have dropped under my stop and told me the whole March-to-August advance was in doubt. That is how I think about a retracement: not as a magic number, but as a ruler laid against the move that came before.

Then there is the matter of who is trading the stock. Foreign institutions held 3.71 per cent in December 2023 and hold 1.49 per cent today. Domestic institutions went from 0.56 to 2.11 per cent. The number of shareholders rose from about 15,700 to 26,300. Put plainly, the stock rose to ₹2,931 on a base of retail investors and a few domestic funds, with the promoter holding 68.34 per cent and not trading. With about 18,000 shares a day changing hands, you could say the stock has the liquidity of a village market. That does not make it bad, but it means prices overshoot in both directions.

Finally, a word about relative strength, which is the polite name for asking whether a stock is beating or trailing the market. Against the Nifty, MPS has lagged by about 27 per cent over 28 days and 23 per cent over 63 days. Against its three listed peers it is still the winner over a year, since all of them are down 18 to 56 per cent. I find that combination oddly comforting and oddly worrying. Comforting, because the market has been telling the difference between this business and its competitors. Worrying, because a leader that has begun to roll over is usually the last domino and not the first.

book_callouts.title: Why a thin stock needs limit prices
book_callouts.quote: A level that is tested twice and holds twice is worth writing down.
book_callouts.text: With roughly ₹4 Cr changing hands on an average day, a single large order can move MPS several per cent, and a stop-loss that fires on an intraday spike can hand the position to a market maker at the worst price. Our own first fill, about ₹1.4 lakh, is tiny compared with the day's turnover, so size is not the problem. Speed and spikes are.
bullets: Enter and exit with limit prices, never at market.
Judge the ₹2,005 stop on a daily close, not on an intraday print.
Work each tranche over several sessions rather than in one clip.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: The leader that stopped leading
book_callouts.quote: A leader that stops leading is not a laggard, yet it is no longer the stock to chase.
book_callouts.text: Over a year MPS is flat while Datamatics, NIIT Learning Systems and Newgen are down between 18 and 56 per cent. It is the best of a poor group. But over the last three months it has fallen about as far as they have, and its relative strength against the Nifty is a negative 27 per cent over 28 days. The best names crack last, and they crack from a higher price.
bullets: MPS is not on the weekly list of 465 Stage 2 stocks.
None of the three listed peers is either; all are in Stage 4.
Waiting costs little, because many other stocks have better charts.

book_subsections.title: The stock's own history: three halvings and a ten-bagger
paragraphs: Let me walk you through the stock's life since 2015, because it is the best argument I have for patience. In April 2015 the shares peaked at ₹1,022. Over the next 46 months they fell to ₹432, a drop of 57.7 per cent. The reasons were ordinary and cumulative: a large amount of cash raised in 2015 that sat idle, a year in which sales fell, and then the acquisition of Tata Interactive in 2018, which dragged the margin from 33 to 26 per cent before it was restructured. The trailing earnings multiple went from 31 times to 11.5 times.

Then came the part that nobody who lived through it forgets. From a November 2019 weekly close of ₹588, the stock lost 67.5 per cent in under five months to ₹191. FY20 had brought price cuts, vendor consolidation and a platform customer moving work back to its own captive, and then Covid arrived. At ₹191 the stock traded at 4.7 times earnings. And yet five years later, in March 2025, it stood at ₹2,898, a gain of 1,416 per cent. HighWire, the eLearning restructuring, the buyback, Liberate, AJE and a return on capital that reached 41 per cent made one of the best compounding runs on the exchange.

Then the third halving: 51.9 per cent in 11 months, from ₹2,898 to ₹1,393 in March 2026, as AJE revenue shrank, Corporate Learning fell, and the whole listed peer group was marked down. The multiple went from 41.7 times to 16.0 times. And then, within five months and on one very good quarter, the stock doubled again to ₹2,931, a multiple of 28.9 times. Today, at 22.7 times, it sits at the five-year median.

What does a mentor take from that? That the stock does not move with the business, it moves with what the market is willing to pay for the business, and that willingness swings between 5 and 42 times earnings. Three drawdowns of more than 50 per cent in eleven years is not a flaw in the stock. It is the price of owning a high-return compounder in a thinly traded corner of the market. And that is why the first fill is capped at half of what the tier would allow, split into two unequal tranches, with two-thirds as the core order at ₹2,070 and the smaller third at ₹2,150 only if the numbers allow, with the rest held back until the chart has turned and the numbers have been redone.

book_subsections.title: The entry zone, and why the stop sits where it does
paragraphs: Here is how I arrived at ₹2,070 to ₹2,150. The upper edge, ₹2,152, is the low the stock made on 27 October and nearly repeated on 4 November. It also happens to be where half of the March-to-August advance has been given back, which is a level that technicians watch. The lower edge, ₹2,069, is the rising 200-day average, and the TradingView monthly support at ₹2,066 lines up with it to within rupees. Four independent measurements in a band about 4 per cent wide is not a coincidence; it is a floor.

The stop at ₹2,005 sits below that floor by about half of one day's typical range. It is 6.74 per cent below ₹2,150. If the price closes beneath it, the 200-day average has failed, the second shelf at ₹1,964 is probably going as well, and the nearest meaningful support is ₹1,811. I would rather admit I was early and step aside than average down into a Stage 4 decline. The CFO told the Q2 FY27 call, “we expect FY27 EBITDA to be at least INR310 crores,” and the business may well deliver that. A stock can still fall while a business delivers, as the 4 November session showed.

The arithmetic of patience has two versions, and I want you to see both. The first values the business on the earnings it should have reported over the twelve months to November 2027, at 18 times. That gives a base value of ₹2,410. The stricter version uses the last full fiscal year's earnings, FY27, with the same multiples. That gives ₹2,241. From ₹2,070 the reward is more than five times the risk to the stop on the first version and about 2.6 times on the second. From ₹2,150 it is about 1.8 times on the first and only about 0.6 on the second. From today's ₹2,297 it is about 0.4 on the first and negative on the second. That is why the ₹2,070 order is the core and the ₹2,150 order is conditional. The business passes the test, and the price, today, does not.

You may ask how I can respect a Stage 4 warning and still leave limit prices in the market. They are different trades. The warning forbids buying at today's price or on a bounce. The ₹2,070 limit is the core, and the ₹2,150 limit is conditional. Both are a half-size, counter-trend entry at the rising 200-day average, inside a long-term uptrend, taken only where the reward is clearly larger than the risk. I abandon it if the daily close breaks ₹2,005. It is not a claim that the trend has turned.

book_subsections.title: What would change my mind, and what I will not do
paragraphs: I will change my view in two directions. If the stock closes a week above the thirty-week average with the ten-week average turning up and volume at least twice its recent norm, or closes a week above the falling fifty-day average near ₹2,500, I will treat it as a candidate for a fresh re-underwrite. That does not release the rest of the position automatically. I will redo the base value from the latest results, re-base the stop, and add only if the reward is at least one and a half times the risk. At ₹2,500 today's base value of ₹2,410 would give a negative reward. If instead it closes a day under ₹2,005, I will treat the decline as confirmed, cancel the alert and look at ₹1,811 and the March base at ₹1,336 to ₹1,393 as places to start watching again, not as places to buy.

What I will not do is chase. The CEO told the Q2 FY27 call, “I would rather miss a deal than overpay,” and I intend to hold myself to the same rule with the shares. He was talking about acquisitions, but the logic is the same. There will always be another entry point for a business that is this good, and there will not always be another chance to avoid a bad one.

Chapter 9 now takes everything in these pages, the tape, the flows, the cycles and the zone, and puts it next to the valuation to give the verdict and the sizing. You already know where it is heading.
